hero.title: Running the event that grows the region.
hero.subtitle: GEarheads host the Wisconsin FTC Rookie Qualifier — giving new teams their first competitive experience in a low-pressure, high-support environment. In our second year running the event, we recruited 3 new FTC judges, partnered with Team 13201 Hazmat, and hosted 26 rookie teams with more than 80 volunteers on the floor.

heroPhoto.caption: Event floor at the 2026 Wisconsin FTC Rookie Qualifier

impact.label: Why it matters
impact.text: Most rookie FTC teams have never seen a real competitive field before their first qualifier. The Rookie Qualifier changes that. By hosting a dedicated event for first-year teams — supported by experienced volunteers, extra Field Technical Advisors, and an on-demand coaching system — we give those teams the runway they need to find their footing before the stakes get higher. Every team that competes here earns a real shot at advancing to the state championship.

approach.label: Our Approach
approach.heading: Why we run the qualifier
approach.body:
Wisconsin's FTC region loses teams every year — not because the teams stop caring, but because the first qualifier is overwhelming. Pit confusion, judging anxiety, alliance selection mystery: these are fixable problems. We built the Rookie Qualifier because GEarheads knows first-hand how much a supportive first event changes a team's trajectory.

Lowering the barrier for new teams is a long-term investment in the region. Every rookie team that has a good first event comes back next season, brings new members, mentors the next cohort of rookies, and eventually trains the region's next generation of judges and FTAs. The compounding value of one well-run event is enormous.

We run the qualifier to the same competitive standards as any sanctioned FTC event — real rankings, real alliance selection, real state-qualification slots. High support does not mean low stakes. The difference is that we surround every team with people who have been exactly where they are, and who want them to succeed.

webinars.label: Competition Flow
webinars.summary: What actually happens on event day, from load-in to alliance selection.
webinars.detail: For a team that has never been to a qualifier, the sheer pace of event day is disorienting. Pits open, inspection queues form, practice matches run, qualification rounds start — and the schedule waits for no one. Our first webinar lays out the complete arc of a competition day in explicit, chronological detail so that no team is blindsided by a process they didn't know existed. We walk through what happens in the pit crew area versus at the field, how a match is called, what the MC and field supervisor roles are, and where to find real-time scoring. Teams leave with a mental map of event day so they can focus their energy on their robot rather than on figuring out where to be.
highlights: Full chronological walkthrough of an FTC qualifier schedule
Pit operations: layout, power access, tool rules, and inspection flow
Understanding match calling, queuing, and field reset procedures
Where to find live scores, match replays, and alliance standings
Q&A with GEarheads members who have competed at nationals and worlds

webinars.label: Alliance Selection
webinars.summary: How to pick and be picked — the strategy layer most rookie teams miss entirely.
webinars.detail: Alliance selection is one of the most misunderstood phases of an FTC event, and it has ended many rookie teams' advancement hopes not because of their robot, but because of avoidable strategic mistakes. This session covers both sides of the table: what captains are looking for when they pick alliance partners, and how a team with a mid-tier ranking can make itself a compelling choice. We discuss the mechanics of the selection process — how many rounds there are, what happens when a team declines, and how the playoff bracket forms — and then move into practical strategy: which autonomous routines, endgame capabilities, and driver behaviors consistently catch the eye of alliance captains. We also cover what to do if you are not picked, and why that outcome is not the end of the road.
highlights: Step-by-step mechanics of the FTC alliance selection process
What captains look for: reliability, auto consistency, endgame capability
How to present your robot's strengths during pit scouting conversations
Handling a decline and the alternate/captain fallback sequence
Real examples from Wisconsin qualifiers — what swung selections

webinars.label: Judging
webinars.summary: How judged awards work, what judges are actually evaluating, and how to prepare.
webinars.detail: The judged awards — Think, Connect, Innovate, Design, and the coveted Inspire Award — represent more than half of what FTC rewards, yet most rookie teams put nearly all their preparation time into the robot and almost none into their judging presentation. This webinar demystifies the process from the judges' perspective. We cover what a judging panel looks for across each award category, how to structure a five-minute presentation that communicates both technical depth and community impact, and how to answer follow-up questions confidently. We also address common rookie mistakes: presentations that are too rehearsed to feel genuine, portfolios that front-load the engineering log and bury the outreach story, and answers that describe what the robot does rather than why the team made the choices they did. GEarheads have earned Inspire nominations at the state and world level — we share what we learned.
highlights: Overview of all FTC judged awards and their evaluation criteria
How to structure a 5-minute interview-style presentation
Portfolio format: engineering log, outreach story, and team identity
Common rookie mistakes and how to avoid them
Tips from GEarheads' own award-winning presentation experience

webinars.label: Portfolio
webinars.summary: The engineering portfolio: what belongs in it, how to organize it, and what judges actually read.
webinars.detail: The FTC engineering portfolio is both a documentation tool and a storytelling vehicle, and the best ones do both jobs simultaneously. This session gives teams a concrete framework for building a portfolio that reads like a design narrative rather than a collection of meeting notes. We cover what sections are required versus optional, how to present your design decisions with evidence (photos, data, sketches) rather than just conclusions, and how to use the portfolio to tell the arc of a season — the problems you started with, the iterations you ran, and the outcomes you measured. We pay particular attention to the outreach and community impact sections, which rookie teams consistently underweight. A strong portfolio does not describe what the team did; it makes the reader understand why the choices mattered.
highlights: Required vs. optional portfolio sections explained
How to write design decisions with evidence, not just outcomes
Structuring the engineering log as a design narrative arc
Documenting outreach: depth over volume, impact over activity count
Formatting, photo quality, and length — what actually matters

webinars.label: Packing
webinars.summary: Everything that needs to fit in the van — and why packing right determines how your event starts.
webinars.detail: Showing up to a competition without the right tools, spare parts, or power supplies is not an uncommon rookie mistake — and it is an entirely preventable one. The final webinar in the series covers the logistics that experienced teams have learned through hard experience. We walk through a full pit checklist: what tools are non-negotiable, which spare parts save events (and which are too heavy to justify), how to manage battery rotation, and how to pack the robot for transport without introducing new mechanical problems. We also cover the soft logistics: arrival and load-in timing, how to use the practice match window effectively, and how to set up a pit area that keeps the drive team focused and the pit crew organized. Teams that arrive prepared do not spend the first two hours of an event solving problems they could have solved at home.
highlights: Complete pit checklist: tools, spares, cables, and consumables
Battery management and rotation strategy for a full event day
How to pack the robot safely for transit
Pit area setup — layout, organization, and drive-team communication
Arrival timing, load-in strategy, and using practice matches

eventDay.label: On Event Day
eventDay.heading: Extra support from the moment teams arrive.
eventDay.subtext: The webinar series prepares teams — but the event itself is where preparation meets reality. We staff the Rookie Qualifier differently from a standard qualifier, with additional layers of on-site support specifically designed for teams in their first competitive season.

cards.label: Extra FTAs on the Floor
cards.desc: We bring additional Field Technical Advisors to the event beyond the standard requirement. Rookie teams encounter hardware and software issues that more experienced teams have already worked through — having extra FTAs means there is someone ready to help immediately rather than waiting for a busy inspection queue to clear.

cards.label: On-Demand Coaching
cards.desc: GEarheads members and alumni circulate through the pit area throughout the day offering on-demand technical coaching. Teams can flag down a coach between matches for a quick robot diagnosis, control system advice, or strategy check — no appointment needed, no judgment. The goal is to keep every team on the field and competing.

cards.label: State-Qualification Path
cards.desc: The Rookie Qualifier is a fully sanctioned FTC event. Teams that perform well advance directly to the Wisconsin state championship — the same path as any standard qualifier. We run the event to the same competitive standards, which means high support does not mean low stakes. Every team competes for real.

cards.label: Hazmat Partnership
cards.desc: Team 13201 Hazmat co-runs the event alongside GEarheads, bringing their own judge recruitment network, volunteer coordination experience, and competitive knowledge to the table. The partnership doubles our organizational capacity and gives rookie teams the benefit of two experienced programs' collective expertise.

cards.label: Rookie-Specific Inspection Lane
cards.desc: A dedicated inspection lane staffed by experienced volunteers walks rookie teams through every checklist item step by step. Rather than a pass/fail stamp, teams leave inspection understanding exactly what was checked and why — so they can fix issues confidently and arrive at the field ready to compete.

cards.label: Opening Ceremony Orientation
cards.desc: Before the first match, we run a short all-teams orientation in the competition hall — field layout, match procedure, scoring reminders, and who to ask for help. Experienced teams can skip it; rookie teams who attend consistently report higher confidence through the first two rounds.
